evidence: CDIAL 4435 *gharapāla “house guardian” explicitly gives Hindi gharwālā “husband” and gharwālī “wife”, alongside Sindhi gharavāro. The full survey gharval- household terms fit that compound family; the modern suffix may have been renewed or transmitted regionally.

CDIAL 10066 mārayati explicitly gives the widespread mār- kill/strike verb, including western mārṇā and Hindi mārnā. Survey mar/mara/mariyo forms are ordinary inflections; the kill gloss distinguishes the transitive verb from the related die paradigm.

CDIAL 8179 pitṛ explicitly gives nominative pitā and Middle Indo-Aryan piu, followed by Punjabi peo/piu and Lahnda pio “father”. The survey pe/pio and learned pitā forms identify this kinship family without equating them with unrelated nursery terms.

CDIAL 6141 dadāti explicitly describes the give paradigm’s dēti and dēhi remodeling and regional deh/de/do forms. Past-only di may instead require the separately treated participial family, so that ambiguity is retained.

CDIAL 4918 cōkṣa gives Sindhi cokho and Gujarati cokhā “cleaned rice”, alongside the pure/clean/good adjective. The survey rice forms support this semantic specialization; the underlying food sense is explicitly attested, not inferred solely from clean.

CDIAL 9828 manuṣya documents manus and Palula meš, while explicitly qualifying several māś/moš forms through mānuṣa or martya. The clear manus/paradigmatic forms can be linked; unresolved short forms retain the competing-root qualification.

CDIAL 9198.1 *bā “father” explicitly gives Nepali bā and bājyā “grandfather”. Its mother branch is separately numbered 9198.2 *bāī; sister or honorific woman senses require distinguishing other bāī families.

CDIAL 1135.1 ātman explicitly gives Hindi āp respectful “you”, Punjabi āpā̃ “we” and Old Marwari āpa “self, you, we”. These survey pronouns belong to the reflexive-to-personal paradigm; the distinct possessive *ātmanaka subsection is not selected.
CDIAL 3164 kim explicitly gives northern and eastern ki/kī “what”, Hindi and Kumauni kyā, and Middle Indo-Aryan ki/kiṃ. The interrogative sense excludes the borrowed Persian conjunction ki.

CDIAL 2528 ēvam ēva discusses kab/kabe and jab only as formations crossed with interrogative ka or relative ya. The unsplit now/just-so parent alone omits this essential pronominal component; a compound or precise construction analysis is needed.

CDIAL 5239 jīva explicitly includes Nepali jiu “body, life”, Oriya jī “heart” and the addendum’s Western Pahari jiu “mind, heart, person”. The survey jiv/jiu body/heart polysemy therefore has primary comparative support.

CDIAL 13574 separately numbers sūra, sūrya and sūriya. The survey suraj/suruj forms contain additional j material absent from the bare sūra parent, and suriya selects its separately numbered branch; these cannot be copied to the broad head.

CDIAL 11580 vālukā gives Hindi bārū, regional bālu and an explicit suffix replacement vālikā accounting for Bengali/Oriya bāli “sand”. No separate stored vālikā subsection exists; the evidence specifies that replacement for i-ending forms.

CDIAL 9883 markaṭa² explicitly gives Hindi makṛī, Punjabi makkaṛī, Nepali mākuro and Oriya makaṛā “spider”. The survey k-r/ḍ spider variants fit the documented family; its relation to other insect-name reconstructions remains qualified.

CDIAL 5071 *chōṭṭa explicitly gives Hindi choṭā, Nepali choṭo and Kashmiri choṭ “short, small”. The selected small/short responses fit this lexical family, while the addendum distinguishes unaspirated *cōṭa and other child-name formations.

CDIAL 5090 separates short-vowel jaḍa, geminate *jaḍḍa and u-vowel *jūḍa. Its section 4 explicitly gives Maithili jūṛ/jūr and Hindi jūṛ “cold”; a-vowel jar without decisive quantity/local evidence remains ambiguous between the first two branches.

CDIAL 8265 putra explicitly gives put/puttar/pūt and northern pūc̣/pūṣ, alongside Palula putr and the wider son family. Punjabi-mediated puttar is explicitly allowed by the addendum; a bare pū requires separate local contraction evidence.

CDIAL 6495 dūra gives dūr/dūri/dūro “far” and explicitly records retroflex ḍūr in the addendum. The simple survey forms fit; dūrāī contains additional nominalizing material whose analysis remains separate.
CDIAL 12278 śata explicitly gives Bengali sa, Marathi śẽ, Maiya/Shina šal and western sau “hundred”. These numeral forms identify the family; no composite hundred-and numeral is included.

CDIAL 9188 bahukāra gives buhārī/bahārī/bohārī “broom”, but very contracted bari may also converge with the vardhanī broom family. Retained buh/bahār material supports the first family; the contracted forms remain a competing-root question.

CDIAL 6010 gives Punjabi tāgā/taggā, Hindi/Bengali tāgā and Nepali tāgā “thread”, from a reconstructed *trāgga/*tārga/*tāgra family. The alternatives concern the reconstructed cluster; all selected survey forms continue the same documented thread family.

CDIAL 9349 bhaginī explicitly gives the bahin/bhaṇ/bheṇ “sister” family and discusses honorific address to women, but bare bai can converge with the nursery bāī family. The n-bearing sister forms are distinguishable; bare bai woman forms require local historical evidence.

CDIAL 6770.1 *dhāgga gives Hindi dhāgā, Nepali dhāgo and Punjabi dhāggā “thread”. The addendum revises the deeper reconstruction toward *dhārga/*dharga; this family link retains that uncertainty and any intra-IA diffusion.
CDIAL 4137 *gāra explicitly gives Hindi gārā, Nepali gāro and regional gārā “mud, mortar”, retaining a conjectural deeper formation. The survey mud sense fits the documented material noun.
CDIAL 5301.1 jyotsnā explicitly gives Nepali jun, Assamese zon and Halbi jon “moon”, contrasting the separately numbered initial-y *yotsnā branch. The j/z-bearing survey forms select the base branch.
CDIAL 5550 ḍimba explicitly gives Bengali ḍim, Assamese ḍimā and Oriya ḍimba “egg”. Dental transcription in dima is retained as a local phonetic qualification; the egg-word family is identifiable.
CDIAL 9479 bhāṣā gives Middle Indo-Aryan bhāsā “speech, language” and modern bhās/bhāś. Full bhāsā may be learned or renewed across Indo-Aryan; the family link leaves that route open.

CDIAL 4313 gōrūpa gives Prakrit gōru and widespread goru/guru “cow, ox, cattle”, including explicit cow uses in Kumauni, Kashmiri and Hindi. It preserves the full cattle compound rather than linking its modern continuations to bare go.

CDIAL 5090 separates short-vowel jaḍa, geminate *jaḍḍa and u-vowel *jūḍa. Its section 4 explicitly gives Maithili jūṛ/jūr and Hindi jūṛ “cold”; a-vowel jar without decisive quantity/local evidence remains ambiguous between the first two branches.

CDIAL 9875.1 marīca gives miri “pepper”, while section 2 *maricca gives Assamese maris, Bihari mirca/miric and Maithili mircāi. The selected chili terms must preserve this distinction; modern pepper-to-chili semantic transfer is explicitly represented by the cited comparanda.

CDIAL 11366 vartman gives bāṭ/vāṭ “path” but expressly states that some feminine forms may equally derive from vartis. That alternative must be checked locally before assigning the existing broad path link.
